title: Projects
text:
The posts on this site are arguments. These are artifacts: code that someone other than me runs, or was built to be handed over. Each one links to its source.
Where a project produced a result, the result is stated here rather than implied — including where the answer was less clean than I wanted.

title: Projects
text:
Research and modelling

Messi vs Ronaldo — the weighted case





An R Shiny dashboard that compares the two on difficulty-adjusted scoring rather than raw totals. Opponent Elo, venue, competition stage and away status are compressed into one difficulty score by a single global FAMD, and goals are weighted by it. The denominator is every valid minute — 2,201 appearances and 181,081 minutes, with all 1,063 scoreless appearances kept in, which is where most comparisons quietly cheat.
The result is the reason the project is worth reading. On the weighted index per 90 the gap is +0.0953 in Messi’s favour (0.1337 against 0.0384), and a seeded 10,000-resample match bootstrap puts 96% of resampled differences above zero — but the 95% percentile interval is [−0.0120, +0.1999], which crosses it. The dashboard reports both numbers side by side and refuses to print a significance verdict or a winner badge. Cohen’s d is +0.090.
It is a fixed 2002–2026 research snapshot, not a live feed of career totals, and the limitations section says so in seven bullets. Runs from a precomputed bundle rather than scraping at startup; the container is pinned by digest and runs non-root.
Open the live dashboard




Bayesian Change-Point Detection in Nigerian Rainfall





A hierarchical Bayesian change-point analysis of 74 years of precipitation (1950–2023) across nine meteorological stations in Nigeria’s three climate zones, written for an IEEE conference paper. PyMC and NUTS, with partial pooling of change-point timing across zones through shared hyperpriors and a non-centered parameterisation.
The finding worth stating: the transitions are coherent but asynchronous — Sahel breaks in 1958, Guinea Savanna in 2016, Coastal in 2015, with the hierarchical group estimate at 1989. The Coastal 94% HDI spans 1996–2022, which is wide enough to be honest about how little that zone’s timing is pinned down. The no-change-point null is decisively rejected in every zone by PSIS-LOO.
Priors are weakly informative and each one is justified in a table in the README. Pre-computed MCMC traces ship with the repository, so the figures can be regenerated without re-running the sampler — the same instinct as _freeze on this site.




Soccer: Bayesian World Cup prediction





Europe versus South America, worked as a causal problem before a predictive one. Currently at stage one: the causal DAG, the implied conditional independencies, and an explicit identification statement, with latent team strength modelled as an unobserved node.
Early and incomplete — the DAG and its validation exist, the model does not yet. It is here because the ordering is the point: the identification argument is written down before anything is fitted.

title: Projects
section: Software built for someone else to use
text:
Software built for someone else to use

ATBU Academic Planning Portal





A desktop application managing 223 professor records for the Director of Academic Planning at Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University. Python and Flet over SQLite, packaged as a Windows executable for a non-technical user.
The part that mattered was the export: the National Universities Commission requires a specific Excel layout for professor-list updates, and producing it by hand for accreditation is where the errors were coming from. The app generates it directly, and imports the three-section Excel format the university already used. Editing is password-protected with bcrypt, and the database backs up in one click.




PRP Command Center





A single-file, zero-dependency operations dashboard covering 20 local government areas and 212 wards in Bauchi State, with real GRID3 geography rendered as inline SVG.
The constraint drove the design: no network requests at all, so it works on a laptop in a room with no connection, which is the room it was built for. Ward status is derived from the clock rather than fetched.




Kaduna Solar Lead Gen





A Streamlit app that pulls real business locations from OpenStreetMap and turns them into qualified solar-installation leads with a generated pitch per prospect.

Silman endgame Anki deck





A generator that turns Jeremy Silman’s Complete Endgame Course into 3,214 Anki flashcards, graded from beginner to expert so the deck can be studied in the rating-band order the book is organised around. Written because I wanted to drill the endgames and typing them by hand was not going to happen.




This website





The source of everything you are reading, execution cache included. Posts run in R or Python, one engine per post, and every published result is frozen at publication so a package upgrade cannot silently change a figure years later.



More work — including client and consultancy material that is not open source — is in my portfolio folder, and anything public is on GitHub.

title: Which Nigerian states got worse, and their deadliest months
text:
Question
“Nigeria is getting worse” is one number, and nothing in it says where. Which states got worse, and which months were deadliest?

title: Which Nigerian states got worse, and their deadliest months
text:
Claim

Nyanya bus station, Abuja, after the 2014 bombing. VOA / Wikimedia Commons, public domain
The headline is true. 29,300 events and 94,586 deaths, 2015 to 2025 (data). A national rate of +22.9 per cent a year (model).
It is also the least useful number in the file.

title: Which Nigerian states got worse, and their deadliest months
text:
Counter-claim
Two facts a national average cannot carry.
The state with the most deaths is not the state worsening fastest (model). And a deadlier month is not a busier one (data).

title: Which Nigerian states got worse, and their deadliest months
text:
Setup
One row per state, LGA, year and month: 772 cells, 37 states, 2015 to 2026 (data). The analysis fits 2015 to 2025. 2026 is six months and still being revised, so it sits out.
Every number is tagged: (data) counted in the file, (model) fitted, (proof) arithmetic.

Show the analysissource("analysis.R")

pal <- c(worse = "#0f766e", flat = "#6b7280", deaths = "#b45309",
         events = "#0e7490", ink = "#57606a")
grid <- "#d7dce1"

title: Which Nigerian states got worse, and their deadliest months
text:
The analysis
Thirty-seven speeds, one direction
The national rate is the middle of a wide spread. State trends run from +1.5 to +59.8 per cent a year (model), a standard deviation of 14.5 points (model). Thirty-three states are worse than flat. Four are flat, and none improves (model).
Sokoto leads at +59.8 per cent (model). Its toll in eleven years is 2,372 deaths (data). Borno’s is 35,355 (data).







Figure 1: Thirty-seven speeds. Borno, the deadliest state, is fifth from the bottom.



Pattern: every interval but four sits right of zero; the spread is nearly the size of the national trend itself.
The deadliest state is not the fastest
Borno is +8.9 per cent a year (model), the third slowest in the country. It carries 30 per cent of all deaths since 2019 (data).
Rank the states by toll and by speed, and the lists barely overlap: rank correlation 0.21 (model). The fastest risers are small: Kwara has 430 deaths in eleven years (data), one-eightieth of Borno’s.







Figure 2: Speed against size. The biggest risers are not the biggest tolls.



Pattern: Borno sits far right and low; the high points sit left. Bigger is not faster.
Ten of the twelve deadliest months are Borno
The top twelve state-months by deaths, 2019 to 2025, are overwhelmingly one state: ten are Borno, and they hold 84 per cent of those deaths (data).
The exception is the point of the chart. Niger, March 2022: 491 deaths from 28 events (data), 17.5 per event, against Borno’s 5 to 12. One LGA, Mariga, took 302 of them in five events (data).
Across states, events and deaths rank together at 0.86 (data). Events and deaths per event rank at 0.39 (data). Busy and lethal are not the same list.







Figure 3: Twelve deadliest state-months. Ten are Borno; the exception is a single month in Niger.



Pattern: one colour fills ten rows. The odd row is not a big month; it is a lethal one.
Deaths have a season; events do not
Events by calendar month are flat: 288 to 320 a month, on average, across equal years (data). Deaths are not. January to June average 891 deaths a month-year; July to October, 700 (data). Ratio 1.27, on the same years.
Both series are indexed to their own mean, so the shapes compare directly (proof).







Figure 4: Deaths rise in the first half; events are a flat line.



Pattern: the bars bow upward in the first half; the line does not move.






NoteWhere the numbers come from





The file. Kaggle justtryit01/nigerian-insecurity-analysis-1997-2026, MIT licence, compiled from ACLED (1997–2026) and UCDP (1990–2024) via HDX. The version here is acled_cleaned.csv, filtered to 2015–2026 and committed as data/acled_clean_lga_month.csv: 106,536 rows, balanced, no duplicates, no negatives. data/PROVENANCE.md records the source and the filter. 84.8 per cent of these LGA-months record no events, which is why the trend model is a count model rather than a line through totals.
The model. One negative binomial with a state-varying slope, pv_events ~ t + (1 + t | state) on the state-month panel, 37 × 132 rows, fitted with glmmTMB. The state estimate is the country slope plus that state’s conditional mode; the interval is the conditional standard deviation, so a small state’s trend is pulled toward the national one and a large state’s is left alone. The national rate is the fixed effect. analysis.R reproduces every number here and caches the one fit that takes time; delete cache/ to refit.
“Worse”, three ways. A state is worse when its interval excludes zero: 33 states. Requiring +10 per cent a year as well: 31. Applying Benjamini–Hochberg across the 37: 33. The post reports the first; the other two are in analysis.R, because the list shrinking under a stricter rule is a fact about the rule, not about Nigeria.
The deadliest months. Ranked on 2019–2025. 2026 is excluded deliberately: it holds six months, its June is thin (131 events against May’s 643), and ACLED revises recent months, so a 2026 month would win or lose this table on reporting lag rather than on deaths.
Caveats that belong here, not in a footnote. ACLED coverage deepens over time, so 2015 and 2025 are not the same reporting regime. Fatality counts in mass-casualty banditry are less reliable than event counts. There is no population column, so “worse” is per area, not per capita. The file carries no actors, event types, coordinates or exact dates, so “banditry against Borno” is not answerable from it.
What this post does not do. No forecast, no held-out score, no model comparison. The specification for that work is nigeria-conflict-methods-spec.md; this post is the descriptive pass that comes before it.





So the country is getting worse.

It is, and the average is the part that misleads. Borno carries one death in three and has barely moved since 2015. The fastest risers are small states with a fraction of its toll. Rank by speed and you get the north-west. Rank by deaths and you get Borno. Both lists are the country.

title: Which Nigerian states got worse, and their deadliest months
text:
The formulas, said twice
Every number above comes out of one model. Here is the model, and here is what each line of it means.


\[\begin{aligned} Y_{st} &\sim \mathrm{NB}_2(\mu_{st},\theta)\\ \log \mu_{st} &= \alpha+\beta t+a_s+b_s t \end{aligned}\]


Events in state \(s\) and month \(t\) are a negative binomial count — a Poisson whose variance is allowed to exceed its mean, which matters when a state has months of five events and months of five hundred. The log link keeps the fitted count positive.


\[(a_s,b_s)\sim N(\mathbf 0,\Sigma)\]


Each state gets its own level and its own trend, drawn from one distribution rather than estimated in isolation. That is what lets a small state borrow strength from the others, and it is why the state estimates are shrunk slightly toward the national line.


\[\beta_s=\beta+b_s,\qquad 100\left(e^{\beta_s}-1\right)\]


The percentage a year. A slope of \(\beta_s\) on a log scale is a growth rate, and a growth rate only becomes a per cent change once it is exponentiated: +22.9 nationally, +59.8 in Sokoto, +8.9 in Borno.


\[100\left(e^{\beta_s\,\pm\,1.96\,se_s}-1\right)\]


The interval, on the same per cent scale — the horizontal lines in the first figure. A state counts as worse when the whole interval is right of zero, which is thirty-three of thirty-seven.


\[\rho_S\big(\beta_s,\; D_s\big)=0.21\]


Spearman’s rank correlation between how fast a state is rising and how many deaths it has had. Almost none, which is the whole of the second section: the fastest states are not the deadliest states.

title: Book revisions
text:
Statistical Inference (2nd ed.)Casella & Berger





All of StatisticsLarry Wasserman





Mathematical Statistics with Applications (7th ed.)Wackerly, Mendenhall & Scheaffer



The texts are Casella & Berger’s Statistical Inference, Wasserman’s All of Statistics and Wackerly, Mendenhall & Scheaffer’s Mathematical Statistics with Applications — a course text, a concise graduate tour, and the applied standard, which between them cover most of where a derivation goes wrong.
Standard texts are often precise at the cost of being unreadable. These posts take one topic at a time and rewrite it: plain statement first, simulation where a simulation makes the point better than an algebraic derivation, and the derivation kept only where it is genuinely the shortest route.
















The standard error, derived in bands



book-revisions



Casella and Berger get Var(X-bar) = sigma squared over n from one expansion and one substitution. Here every equation carries its own numbered R line, in seven bands — ending with the check, the plug-in, Efron’s bootstrap, and why quartering the error needs quadrupling the sample.





2026-08-10

15 min

title: Jerry Bannister Zachary
text:
My ideas, AI’s implementation — I fuse the two, and I am a transhumanist about where that leads.
I am a statistician at Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University in Bauchi, Nigeria, where I am a Senior Statistician in the Academic Planning & Quality Assurance unit — building the institutional databases that sixty-odd departments report into, and advising the research projects that pass through them. Since 2017 I have also run JJMB Datascience Hub, an independent consultancy doing much the same work for clients in public health, finance and academia.
I am currently a PhD student in Statistics at ATBU, working on hybrid Bayesian deep learning for spatio-temporal risk forecasting. My MSc is also from ATBU and my BSc from the University of Maiduguri, finishing in at least the top two of my class in both instances. I put it that way on purpose. I am strongly against the GPA system: it compresses years of uneven and largely incomparable work into one number, and then invites everybody to treat that number as a finding rather than as the very lossy summary it is. Rank is the least misleading version I can give, and the actual evidence is the work — the posts here and my projects.
My interest is in statistics as a whole — every method in it, not a chosen subset of favourites. The fuller range is below.
This site is where I check that work instead of assuming it. A simulation that disagrees with what I expected is the most useful thing I can publish, so most of what is here is written to be run again rather than read once.

title: Jerry Bannister Zachary
text:
Areas I work in
A map of the ground, not a claim to have covered all of it. Where something here has a post behind it, the post is the evidence; where it does not, read it as interest rather than track record. Each domain opens only if you want it.


Statisticsinference, Bayesian, regression, survival, time series, spatial, causal


Foundations — probability and distribution theory, asymptotics, estimation theory (maximum likelihood, moments, M-estimation), sufficiency, information and decision theory
Inference — hypothesis tests, confidence and credible intervals, likelihood-ratio/Wald/score, power and sample size, multiple comparisons and FDR, equivalence testing
Bayesian — priors, elicitation and conjugate analysis, MCMC (Metropolis–Hastings, Gibbs, HMC/NUTS), variational inference, ABC, hierarchical and multilevel models, posterior predictive checks, LOO-CV, WAIC, Bayes factors, model averaging
Regression — linear, GLM, GAM, mixed-effects and GLMM, quantile, robust, ridge/lasso/elastic net, splines, nonlinear regression, overdispersion; logistic, ordinal and multinomial; Poisson, negative binomial, zero-inflated and hurdle models

Time series — ARIMA/SARIMA/ARIMAX, exponential smoothing, state-space and Kalman filtering, structural time series, VAR/VECM and cointegration, GARCH, spectral analysis, change-point detection, probabilistic forecasting and backtesting
Spatial — geostatistics and kriging, variograms, CAR and SAR, INLA, point processes, geo-additive models, disease mapping, small-area estimation

Design and surveys — RCTs, factorial and fractional factorial, blocking, split-plot, crossover, response surface, optimal design, A/B and sequential designs; sampling designs, stratification and clustering, complex weighting, raking, non-response, design-based variance, questionnaire design
Missing data and resampling — MCAR/MAR/MNAR, multiple imputation, EM, weighting, sensitivity analysis; bootstrap, jackknife, permutation tests, cross-validation, Monte Carlo, simulation study design
Nonparametrics and applied fields — rank-based tests, kernel density estimation, nonparametric regression, empirical likelihood; biostatistics and epidemiology, econometrics and panel data, psychometrics and IRT, reliability and extreme values, statistical process control, meta-analysis, demography, actuarial and risk modelling
Specialised data — compositional, functional data analysis, directional and circular statistics, network data, longitudinal and panel data

Supervised and ensembles — linear and logistic regression, k-NN, naive Bayes, SVM, discriminant analysis, decision trees; bagging, random forests, extra trees, gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), AdaBoost, stacking and blending

title: How big should the spoon be?
text:
Question
Polls put Peter Obi first; he finished third. At 2,000 interviews the margin is ±2.18 points (proof). The miss was 19.29 points (proof). Was the sample too small?

title: How big should the spoon be?
text:
Claim
On TVC, three weeks before the vote, El-Rufai dismissed the polls:

VOA / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

Opinion polls are distorted… When you have about a 100 million registered voters and you are sampling 2,000 registered voters or 300 registered voters, your results from day one are unreliable; they will have high margins of error.

He was right that they were wrong.

title: How big should the spoon be?
text:
Counter-claim
His next sentence is the better objection.

Most of these polls, like the one by Bloomberg, ANAP and the one by Okonjo Iweala, all used telephone. What percentage of registered voters have phone numbers in INEC’s records? We have found out and it’s 31 per cent.

Only 31 per cent of the register can be telephoned (assume). The simulation prices it. Five hundred, whole register: winner right 3,967 of 4,000 (sim). Forty thousand, phones: winner right 0 of 4,000 (sim).

title: How big should the spoon be?
text:
Setup
NaijaSim is invented: 90,000,000 voters, six zones, four colour-named parties (assume). Phone reach is his 31 per cent (assume). The truth is fixed before anyone is interviewed.

Show the simulationlibrary(plotly)

comma <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  formatC(x, format = "f", big.mark = ",", digits = digits)
}

z <- qnorm(0.975)                        # 95% two-sided

# The post's palette: one hue per stream already exists; these four are the
# parties, and ink is the truth line rather than a party.
pal  <- c("#0f766e", "#0e7490", "#b45309", "#6d28d9")
ink  <- "#57606a"
grid <- "#d7dce1"



Show the simulation# ---- Quoted inputs. Every other number in this post derives from these. ----

# ANAP Foundation / NOIPolls, February 2023; see the method note below.
anap_n <- 2000
poll <- c(Obi = 21, Tinubu = 13, Atiku = 10, Kwankwaso = 3,
          Undecided = 23, Refused = 30)

elrufai_n   <- 40000    # his own poll, as he described it on air
phone_share <- 0.31     # his figure for phone coverage, not checked against INEC

# INEC, 2023 presidential election.
registered  <- 93469008
votes_cast  <- 24965218
votes_valid <- 24025940
votes <- c(Obi = 6101533, Tinubu = 8794726,
           Atiku = 6984520, Kwankwaso = 1496687)

# A mistyped input should fail the render rather than publish quietly.
stopifnot(
  sum(poll) == 100,
  sum(votes) <= votes_valid,
  votes_valid <= votes_cast,
  votes_cast <= registered
)



Show the simulation# Fifty-three of every hundred respondents were undecided or would not say, so the
# headline numbers do not sum to anything like a vote share. Comparing with the
# result means rebasing onto the respondents who named a candidate.
decided  <- sum(poll[names(votes)])
poll_obi <- poll[["Obi"]] / decided
act_obi  <- votes[["Obi"]] / votes_valid
miss     <- poll_obi - act_obi



Show the simulationfpc     <- sqrt((registered - anap_n) / (registered - 1))
se_anap <- sqrt(poll_obi * (1 - poll_obi) / anap_n)



Show the simulation# The sample size at which the margin of error would have been as wide as the
# miss, i.e. the only n for which the objection lands.
n_cross <- ceiling(z^2 * poll_obi * (1 - poll_obi) / miss^2)

title: How big should the spoon be?
text:
The simulation

Show the simulationset.seed(20260817)

sim_party <- c("Green", "Blue", "Red", "Yellow")
sim_zone  <- c("North West", "North East", "North Central",
               "South West", "South East", "South South")
sim_reg_z <- c(21, 12, 15, 18, 9, 15) * 1e6      # registered voters, by zone
names(sim_reg_z) <- sim_zone

# The national result, set by fiat. Blue wins.
sim_target <- c(Green = 0.30, Blue = 0.38, Red = 0.24, Yellow = 0.08)

# Zone shares are chosen, EXCEPT North Central, solved so the register-weighted
# truth lands exactly on sim_target.
sim_zs <- rbind(
  c(0.08, 0.50, 0.36, 0.06),
  c(0.10, 0.52, 0.32, 0.06),
  c(NA,   NA,   NA,   NA  ),
  c(0.34, 0.34, 0.22, 0.10),
  c(0.72, 0.12, 0.08, 0.08),
  c(0.48, 0.26, 0.16, 0.10)
)
dimnames(sim_zs) <- list(sim_zone, sim_party)
i_nc <- match("North Central", sim_zone)
sim_zs[i_nc, ] <- (sum(sim_reg_z) * sim_target -
                   colSums(sim_zs[-i_nc, ] * sim_reg_z[-i_nc])) / sim_reg_z[i_nc]

# Phone reach is chosen, EXCEPT South South, solved so national coverage is
# exactly the 31 per cent he quoted. The poorest zones reach fewest.
sim_reach_z <- c(`North West` = 0.160, `North East` = 0.120,
                 `North Central` = 0.300, `South West` = 0.500,
                 `South East` = 0.440, `South South` = NA)[sim_zone]
i_ss <- match("South South", sim_zone)
sim_reach_z[i_ss] <- (phone_share * sum(sim_reg_z) -
                      sum((sim_reg_z * sim_reach_z)[-i_ss])) / sim_reg_z[i_ss]

# Each zone splits 60/40 into two states leaning opposite ways, so no stratum is
# internally uniform. B moves 1.5x as far as A, preserving the zone average; the
# 0.5 cap keeps every state inside (0, 1).
sim_st <- NULL; sim_reg_s <- numeric(0); sim_szone <- character(0)
for (zn in sim_zone) {
  g <- sim_zs[zn, "Green"]; b <- sim_zs[zn, "Blue"]
  d <- 0.5 * min(g / 1.5, b)
  s_a <- sim_zs[zn, ]; s_a["Green"] <- g + d;       s_a["Blue"] <- b - d
  s_b <- sim_zs[zn, ]; s_b["Green"] <- g - 1.5 * d; s_b["Blue"] <- b + 1.5 * d
  sim_st    <- rbind(sim_st, s_a, s_b)
  sim_reg_s <- c(sim_reg_s, 0.60 * sim_reg_z[[zn]], 0.40 * sim_reg_z[[zn]])
  sim_szone <- c(sim_szone, zn, zn)
}
sim_frame_s <- sim_reg_s * unname(sim_reach_z[sim_szone])

# A mistyped country should fail the render rather than publish quietly.
stopifnot(
  sum(sim_reg_z) == 90e6,
  all(abs(rowSums(sim_st) - 1) < 1e-12),
  all(sim_st > 0), all(sim_st < 1),
  isTRUE(all.equal(colSums(sim_st * sim_reg_s) / sum(sim_reg_s), sim_target)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(sum(sim_frame_s) / sum(sim_reg_s), phone_share))
)

sim_w_true  <- sim_reg_s   / sum(sim_reg_s)     # a fair poll's weights
sim_w_frame <- sim_frame_s / sum(sim_frame_s)   # what a phone poll actually gets
sim_truth   <- colSums(sim_st * sim_w_true)
sim_ptruth  <- colSums(sim_st * sim_w_frame)
sim_frame_N <- sum(sim_frame_s)



Show the simulation# Seeded here, not left to the chunk above, so these numbers do not depend on
# how many draws the country construction happened to consume.
set.seed(20260817)

# Largest remainder: proportional shares rounded the obvious way do not sum to n.
sim_alloc <- function(n, w) {
  raw <- n * w; a <- floor(raw); k <- n - sum(a)
  if (k > 0) { j <- order(raw - a, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(k)]; a[j] <- a[j] + 1 }
  stopifnot(sum(a) == n)
  a
}

SIM_REPS <- 4000

# One rmultinom call per state, vectorised over all 4,000 repetitions.
sim_run <- function(n, w) {
  a <- sim_alloc(n, w)
  est <- matrix(0, SIM_REPS, 4, dimnames = list(NULL, sim_party))
  for (i in seq_along(a)) {
    if (a[i] == 0) next
    est <- est + w[i] * t(rmultinom(SIM_REPS, a[i], sim_st[i, ])) / a[i]
  }
  est
}

# "Right" means Blue tops the poll, not merely Blue ahead of Green.
sim_summ <- function(est) {
  g <- 100 * est[, "Green"]
  c(green = mean(g), sd = sd(g),
    right = 100 * mean(sim_party[max.col(est, ties.method = "first")] == "Blue"))
}

sim_ns_fair  <- c(n_cross, 100, 250, 500, 1000, anap_n)
sim_ns_phone <- c(anap_n, elrufai_n)
sim_fair  <- lapply(sim_ns_fair,  sim_run, w = sim_w_true)
sim_phone <- lapply(sim_ns_phone, sim_run, w = sim_w_frame)
sim_ft    <- t(sapply(sim_fair,  sim_summ))
sim_pt    <- t(sapply(sim_phone, sim_summ))

# Indexed by value, not position, so the prose survives a reordered ladder.
i_win <- match(500, sim_ns_fair)     # the rung the argument turns on
i_2k  <- match(anap_n, sim_ns_fair)
j_2k  <- match(anap_n, sim_ns_phone)
j_40k <- match(elrufai_n, sim_ns_phone)


What a phone frame actually is
Through a phone, Green leads by 3.5 points (sim). In the country, Blue leads by 8 (sim). The figure is not a smaller copy of the country; it is a different country, one that leans Green. Each coloured box is one party’s share. The two groups are the two frames. They are the invented country’s truth, not Nigeria’s result.







Figure 1: A phone frame is a different country, leaning Green.



Pattern: each bar is a party, coloured by its name; the phone frame lifts Green and cuts Blue, while the dotted lines mark the country’s true shares.
The spoon, priced: population size buys nothing
Population size is worth 0.0011% of the margin (proof). That is his objection, priced.







Figure 2: Ninety million voters buy 0.0011% of the margin.



Pattern: the two lines are one line; the shaded sliver is the entire population correction.
Four thousand runs: sample size is not the fix
Five hundred beats forty thousand, eighty times smaller (sim). The frame never climbs. The ladder: Blue tops 4,000 polls 64% of the time at 500 interviews and 100% at 2,000; never, even at 40,000, on the phone frame. The trend is precision, not accuracy. More interviews sharpen a fair poll toward 100 (sim). The phone line never leaves zero (sim).







Figure 3: Bigger spoon, same corner. The frame never wins.



Pattern: one line climbs, the other flatlines at zero — the gap is the frame.
The same answer, harder: precision without accuracy
At 2,000, phones wobble 0.96 points against 0.87 fair (sim). Narrowest, and furthest from the truth.







Figure 4: Narrow, and furthest from the truth.



Pattern: four bell curves, narrowest on the right; the truth lines mark each frame’s centre.






NoteWhere the numbers come from





The margin. For a proportion \(p\) from \(n\) draws, \(SE=\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\). Population size enters only through the finite population correction \(\sqrt{(N-n)/(N-1)}\), which at \(n=2{,}000\) against \(N=93{,}469{,}008\) is 0.9999893 — a shrinkage of 0.0011% of the standard error.
The miss. Obi polled 44.68% of decided respondents and took 25.40% of valid votes: a gap of 19.29 points, or 17.3 standard errors. Inverting the margin for the sample size that would cover a miss that large gives 26 interviews — the rung on the left of the ladder, and the reason the ladder starts there.
The country. NaijaSim is invented and deliberately not a model of Nigeria. Zone names are real; register, zone splits, parties and result are made up, because verifiable zone-level 2023 figures do not exist from one authoritative source and inventing them while calling them the past would be worse than inventing a country and saying so. Ninety million registered, six zones, four colour-named parties, and coverage of 31% borrowed from his own figure. Seeded at 20260817; 4,000 repetitions at each sample size; stratified by state.
Quoted, not derived. The El-Rufai quotations are as reported by The Guardian Nigeria from Journalists’ Hangout on TVC News, 4 February 2023. The sample size, phone-based stratified random method and the six percentages come from ANAP Foundation’s press release; the register and valid votes are INEC’s, via the published breakdown. Outlets differ on the second figure in that first quotation, The Guardian having “300” where The Cable reports “three thousand”; the arithmetic uses ANAP’s published 2,000, so nothing turns on it. His own 40,000-sample poll has no published methodology I could find, and appears here as a sample size and nothing else.
The portrait. File:Nasir Ahmed el-Rufai 2023.jpg on Wikimedia Commons, 470 × 662, tagged PD-VOA: a Voice of America work, so public domain in the United States rather than openly licensed. The Commons page records it as a VOA Africa upload, which is what makes the tag stick.
Attribution, split deliberately. That accuracy depends on absolute sample size rather than on the sampling fraction is standard, and Freedman, Pisani and Purves develop it in the chapter on chance errors in sampling in Statistics. The soup-and-spoon comparison is attributed to George Gallup, not to them, because I could not verify that the book uses the soup wording.





So five hundred people told you who won, and forty thousand did not?

He was half right. The phone polls were wrong, and the simulation agrees every run. But sample size was not why. Forty thousand phone interviews named the winner 0 times in 4,000 (sim). Five hundred from the whole register named it 3,967 times (sim). The spoon was never too small. It never reached the bottom.

title: How big should the spoon be?
text:
The formulas, said twice
The post runs on two pieces of arithmetic: his objection, and the simulation that prices it. Here they are both ways.
His objection, as arithmetic


\[\mathrm{SE}(\hat p)=\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}},\qquad \mathrm{MOE}=z_{0.975}\,\mathrm{SE}\]


The margin depends on \(n\), the number asked — not on \(N\), the number who exist. At 2,000 interviews it is ±2.18 points; at 40,000, ±0.49. Neither is 19 points.


\[\mathrm{fpc}=\sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}\]


The only place the size of the register enters at all. At 2,000 against 93,469,008 it shrinks the margin by 0.0011 per cent — which is why the spoon, not the soup, is what he was describing.


\[n^{\star}=\frac{z^{2}\,\hat p(1-\hat p)}{\text{miss}^{2}}\]


The sample that would have made his sentence true: 26 interviews, against an actual miss of 19.29 points. A poll small enough to miss by that much would be a poll of twenty-six people.


What the simulation computes


\[\hat p_j^{(b)}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf 1\big[\text{voter }k\text{ backs }j\big]\]


One run \(b\), of 4,000. Interview \(n\) people, count who backs each party, and divide by \(n\). The frame decides who the \(n\) people are; nothing else differs between the runs.


\[\hat{\Pr}(\text{right})=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbf 1\big[\text{top party in run } b \text{ is Blue}\big]\]


The number quoted in the text: the share of 4,000 runs whose top party is the true top party. 3,967 of 4,000 at 500 on the register; 0 of 4,000 at 40,000 by phone.


\[\tilde\pi_z=\frac{\pi_z\,r_z}{\sum_{z'}\pi_{z'}\,r_{z'}}\]


The phone frame, in one line. Zone \(z\) is weighted by its phone reach \(r_z\) instead of its population \(\pi_z\). That single substitution is the entire difference between the two countries in the first figure.

title: The standard error, derived in bands
text:
Claim
The standard error of a mean is a number you can derive without imagining a second sample. Casella and Berger do it in §5.2: Theorem 5.2.6(b), p. 214, proves \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n\), and the standard error is its square root.
The proof has one idea, and it is not a clever one. Square the deviation, expand the square into \(n^2\) terms, then take the expectation of the right-hand side term by term: the \(n\) squared terms each expect \(\sigma^2\), and independence forces all \(n(n-1)\) cross terms to expect zero. What survives is \(n\sigma^2\). Divide by \(n^2\) and the \(n\) cancels once, leaving \(\sigma^2/n\).
Everything below is that sentence, with one numbered line of R beside each equation. No step of the derivation is estimated, and no distribution is assumed. Bands 6 and 7 come after the proof is finished: one checks the answer, the other does what a reader actually needs to do with it.

title: The standard error, derived in bands
text:
What it means in English
You took twenty-five measurements and averaged them. The average is not the truth; it is off by something, and the standard error says how big that something usually is. A spread of 1.3 cm per measurement becomes 0.26 cm of error in the average of twenty-five — a factor of 5 smaller, because \(\sqrt{25}=5\).
Four things it is not:


Not the standard deviation of your measurements. That is 1.3 cm, and collecting more data leaves it where it is. The standard error is what shrinks.

Not the variance of the mean. That is 0.0676, in cm². It is the standard error squared, and it is not an error bar.

Not a probability. On its own it is a distance. It becomes “95 per cent of the time” only once you know the shape of the scatter.

Not something the simulation at the end proves. Band 6 runs the experiment and band 7 resamples it; neither is the derivation. Delete both and the theorem stands exactly as written.

Not the same thing as an error bar you can quote. The formula uses \(\sigma\), which you do not know. Replacing it with the sample’s \(s\) is a choice made after the proof, in (7.3), and it costs you some accuracy — this sample’s replacement reads a little high, and honestly so.

title: The standard error, derived in bands
text:
Code, maths, English
Seven bands. Bands 1 to 6 are the theorem and its check; band 7 is what the finished number is for — scaling it, estimating it, bootstrapping it, and turning it into a probability.
Inside a band, each code line L has exactly one equation (b.n) beside it and each equation has exactly one code line, so the map column reads L4 ↔︎ (2.1) in both directions. Definitions are labelled as definitions: where a pair is an assignment rather than a probability statement, the maths uses \(:=\) and the comment says so.








Code
Maths
English



BAND 1 — the three numbers





L1 ↔︎ (1.1) mu <- 5

(1.1) \(\mu := 5\)

A definition, not a measurement. R’s <- and maths’ \(:=\) are the same statement, in two alphabets.



L2 ↔︎ (1.2) sigma <- 1.3

(1.2) \(\sigma := 1.3,\quad\sigma^2 = 1.69\)

1.3 cm is one measurement’s spread. 1.69 is the same fact squared, in cm². They differ by a square root, and that difference is the whole post.



L3 ↔︎ (1.3) n <- 25

(1.3) \(n := 25\)

How many measurements. Fixed by design, not estimated from anything.


BAND 2 — one sample, and its deviations





L4 ↔︎ (2.1) x <- rnorm(n, mu, sigma)

(2.1) \(X_1,\dots,X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(\mu,\sigma^2)\)

25 draws. The normal is a convenient source of independent numbers and nothing more: no later line uses its shape.



L5 ↔︎ (2.2) z <- x - mu

(2.2) \(z_i := X_i - \mu,\qquad E[z_i] = 0\)

Centre each measurement on the truth. After this line \(\mu\) is gone and only \(z\) remains, which is why every later step is short. Note \(z\) is centred on the truth, not on mean(x).


BAND 3 — the square splits into two blocks





L6 ↔︎ (3.1) M <- outer(z, z)

(3.1) \(\Big(\sum_i z_i\Big)^2 = \sum_i z_i^2 + \sum_{i\ne j} z_i z_j\)

Every product of two deviations, all 625 of them, in one 25×25 matrix.



L7 ↔︎ (3.2) sum(diag(M))

(3.2) \(\sum_i z_i^2 \quad\) — \(n\) diagonal terms
prints 66.76. That is this sample’s diagonal block. Hold on to it: band 4 will print something else, and both will be correct.



L8 ↔︎ (3.3) sum(M) - sum(diag(M))

(3.3) \(\sum_{i\ne j} z_i z_j \quad\) — \(n(n-1)\) cross terms
prints 160.7. And 66.76 + 160.7 = 227.4, which is \((\sum z_i)^2\). The split is exact, not approximate.



L9 ↔︎ (3.4) n + n * (n - 1)

(3.4) \(n + n(n-1) = n^2\)

prints 625 — the count, matching the matrix’s 625 cells. \(n\) squares and \(n(n-1)\) crosses, nothing else.


BAND 4 — take the expectation of each block





L10 ↔︎ (4.1) S <- matrix(rnorm(N * n, mu, sigma), N, n) - mu

(4.1) \(N\) independent samples of size \(n\), each centred the same way
100,000 repeats of band 2. This is what “expectation” means when you have to compute it: the same experiment, many times, averaged.



L11 ↔︎ (4.2) mean(rowSums(S^2))

(4.2) \(E\Big[\sum_i z_i^2\Big] = n\sigma^2\)

prints 42.28 ± 0.03782, against \(n\sigma^2 = 42.25\). This is why L7’s 66.76 was not an error: one sample varies, the average over 100,000 does not. Band 4 exists to make that difference undeniable.



L12 ↔︎ (4.3) mean(rowSums(S)^2 - rowSums(S^2))

(4.3) \(E[z_iz_j] = \operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j) = 0,\quad i \ne j\)

prints 0.04796 ± 0.1851 against an exact 0. Zero plus noise. This single line is where independence is used — forget it and the block is a covariance, and the answer is no longer \(\sigma^2/n\).



L13 ↔︎ (4.4) n * sigma^2

(4.4) \(n\sigma^2 = 42.25\)

The exact value L11 was aiming at. No draws, no noise: this is what the algebra delivers before any data exists.


BAND 5 — add the blocks, divide by \(n^2\), then root





L14 ↔︎ (5.1) (1 / n^2) * (n * sigma^2)

(5.1) \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \dfrac{1}{n^2}\,n\sigma^2 = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\)

prints 0.0676, in cm². The two blocks went back together: \(n\sigma^2 + 0 = 42.25\), then the \(1/n^2\) out front, and one \(n\) cancels. That cancellation is Theorem 5.2.6(b).



L15 ↔︎ (5.2) sigma / sqrt(n)

(5.2) \(\operatorname{SE}(\bar X) = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\)

prints 0.26, in cm. Not the same number as (5.1) and not interchangeable with it: one is the other squared. If (5.1) and (5.2) ever look like the same quantity, the units have stopped doing their job.


BAND 6 — check the finished result by simulation





L16 ↔︎ (6.1) means <- replicate(N, mean(rnorm(n, mu, sigma)))

(6.1) \(\bar X_1,\dots,\bar X_N\) from \(N\) independent samples
100,000 averages, each from 25 fresh measurements. This is the experiment the theorem makes a prediction about, run 100,000 times.



L17 ↔︎ (6.2) var(means)

(6.2) \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) \approx \widehat{\operatorname{var}}\big(\{\bar X_k\}\big)\)

prints 0.06734 against the exact 0.0676 — ratio 0.9962. The variance of the averages lands on (5.1).



L18 ↔︎ (6.3) sd(means)

(6.3) \(\operatorname{SE}(\bar X) \approx \widehat{\operatorname{sd}}\big(\{\bar X_k\}\big)\)

prints 0.2595 against the exact 0.26. Rooting L17’s answer, or taking the spread of the 100,000 means, gives the same number to three digits.


BAND 7 — what the number is for





L19 ↔︎ (7.1) sizes <- c(n, 4 * n, 16 * n)

(7.1) \(\operatorname{SE}(\bar X_n) = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\), so \(\operatorname{SE}_{4n} = \tfrac12 \operatorname{SE}_n\) and \(\operatorname{SE}_{16n} = \tfrac14 \operatorname{SE}_n\)

No new derivation: the \(\sqrt n\) from (5.2) is simply read at \(n\), \(4n\) and \(16n\). This is the first question anyone asks after seeing the formula — how much does more data buy?



L20 ↔︎ (7.2) sd_sizes <- sapply(sizes, ...)

(7.2) \(\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}\) at each of the three sizes
prints 0.2589, 0.1297, 0.06467 against 0.26, 0.13, 0.065. Quadruple the sample and the error halves: 1.997 against a predicted 2. Sixteen times the data buys a quarter of the error, not a sixteenth — 4.003 against a predicted 4 — so to halve it again you must quadruple again. Precision is bought with a square root, and that is the bill.



L21 ↔︎ (7.3) se_hat <- sd(x) / sqrt(n)

(7.3) \(\widehat{\operatorname{SE}} = \dfrac{s}{\sqrt n}\), where \(s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (X_i - \bar X)^2\)


\(\sigma\) is never actually known, so \(s\) — the spread of the sample from band 2 — goes in its place. Prints 0.31 against the true 0.26. The gap is not a bug: that sample’s \(s\) is 1.55 cm against \(\sigma = 1.3\), so this sample’s honest error bar really is wider than the truth’s would be. Two numbers, both correct, answering different questions — and band 3 already showed you why this sample is the wide one.



L22 ↔︎ (7.4) boot <- replicate(N, mean(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))

(7.4) \(X^*_1, \dots, X^*_n\) drawn with replacement from \(x\)

Efron’s route: no formula, no \(\sigma\), no imagined fresh data. Resample the twenty-five numbers you already hold, 100,000 times, and keep each average.



L23 ↔︎ (7.5) sd(boot)

(7.5) \(\sqrt{\dfrac{n-1}{n}} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt n}\)

prints 0.3035 against 0.3038 from (7.3) — ratio 0.979, which is \(\sqrt{24/25} = 0.9798\) to four digits. The bootstrap reproduces the plug-in without doing the algebra, and is low by exactly that finite-sample factor. Same answer, different road, and the roads do not quite meet.



L24 ↔︎ (7.6) mean(abs(means - mu) <= 1.96 * se_exact)

(7.6) \(\Pr\big(\lvert \bar X - \mu \rvert \le 1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt n\big) \approx 0.95\)

prints 95.11 per cent. Not the derivation: a distance becomes a probability only once the shape of the scatter is known, which §5.3 and §5.5 supply and §5.2 does not. The check also has to borrow means from band 6, because one sample cannot demonstrate coverage on its own.










NoteWhere this comes from





The derivation. Casella & Berger, Statistical Inference, 2nd ed., §5.2. Lemma 5.2.5 (p. 213) states \(\operatorname{Var}\big(\sum g(X_i)\big)=n\operatorname{Var}g(X_1)\); its proof writes the variance as the expectation of a squared sum and counts \(n\) diagonal and \(n(n-1)\) cross terms. Theorem 4.5.5 makes each cross term a covariance; independence makes it zero. Theorem 5.2.6(b) (p. 214) takes \(g(x)=x/n\), giving \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=n\cdot\sigma^2/n^2=\sigma^2/n\). Bands 2 to 5 are that proof with the expectations written out instead of cited, so that L12 is visibly the step where independence enters and nowhere else.
The name. §5.2 stops at the variance. The words “standard error” do not occur until §10.1.4, “Bootstrap Standard Errors”, p. 478. Taking the square root — (5.2) — is the step every applied text adds and this one does not.
The bootstrap. Efron, B. (1979), “Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife”, Annals of Statistics 7(1), 1–26. For the mean, the variance of the resampling distribution is exactly \(\frac{n-1}{n}\cdot\frac{s^2}{n}\), not approximately so, which is where the \(\sqrt{(n-1)/n}\) in (7.5) comes from and why band 7 can predict the bootstrap’s shortfall before running it.
The code. One chunk, include: false, labelled se-bands. Every number in the table is pulled from it as an inline r expression formatted to four significant figures; none is typed. set.seed(7) fixes the single sample in bands 2, 3 and 7, and set.seed(11) the 100,000 replicates in bands 4, 6 and 7, so the printed values are stable across renders. The scaling check in (7.2) uses N_scale <- 2e4 rather than N, because each of its repeats draws up to sixteen times as many numbers for a claim that is only a ratio; 20,000 repeats pin the ratio to three digits at a tenth of the cost.
About the sample in band 3. It is not typical, and it is not tuned. 66.76 against an expectation of 42.28 is roughly two standard deviations high. That gap is left in deliberately: it is the cleanest instance available of the difference between a realisation and its expectation, and a reader who has just seen both numbers in adjacent bands will not confuse them in band 5. The same wide sample is why the plug-in at (7.3) reads 0.31 where the truth is 0.26.
The photograph. Carl Friedrich Gauss, 1840, by Christian Albrecht Jensen. A faithful photographic reproduction of a two-dimensional public-domain work; the artist died in 1870, and the painting is public domain in its country of origin and in the United States. Via Wikimedia Commons; cropped to a portrait, nothing else altered.

title: Simulations
text:
